newsitem.title: FINLAND: Euro-Finns flex new muscles, tackle taboos.
newsitem.headline: Euro-Finns flex new muscles, tackle taboos.

text.p: An apparently technical move by Finland into Europe's currency stability mechanism at the weekend shows a country for centuries overshadowed by the might of its larger neighbours flexing new-found political muscle.

Its decision to link its currency to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism was one of Finland's first major political moves independent of either Sweden to the west, or Russia to the east. It demonstrated Finland is out of its Cold War isolation.

"We have to play this ball in Europe," Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said in an interview with the Finnish STT news agency on Sunday. "We can't just pass the ball around in some corner with a few neighbours. We have to score goals."

Finland, under Russian rule until 80 years ago, joined the European Union with Sweden in 1995. Its five million population voted before Sweden to join, but the official decision only came after Sweden had moved.

For decades, Finland's closeness to the former Soviet Union muffled debate in this Nordic country, but recently politicians and the media have started venturing on to the previously taboo topics of Finland's broad foreign policy.
"I have not said that we should in any case join NATO," said senior foreign policy commentator Max Jacobson in the daily Aamulehti on Sunday.

Highly influential, he stirred a storm of controversy earlier this year by raising the possibility that Finland -- and other neutral countries, Sweden and Austria -- may end up joining the western military alliance.
That question is the hot topic Finland may next tackle. For the moment, the fact that it is even discussed in public is controversial enough.
During the Cold War Finland adopted a neutral military stance alongside Sweden. Its leaders sometimes struggled to reconcile this with at times overbearing influence from Moscow.

Now in the European Union, official Finland has changed neutral to "non-aligned" and stressed that it sees membership of the Union -- and with it of a single currency in 1999 -- as a fundamental boost to its security.

"If, by a stretch of the imagination, Russia were to become aggressive, then it would be much more difficult for Russia to threaten EU-member Finland than it was," said parliament member Jukka Tarkka of the liberal Progressive Finnish Party.
On these grounds, Finland's leaders say it has no need of the security guarantees the Western alliance offers.
But as NATO's relationship with Russia and eastern Europe develops, analysts argue Finland should expect to adapt.
"My point is that a significant change is certainly under way," Jakobson said. "A new security system is emerging, the core of which will be NATO and a cooperation mechanism between NATO and Russia."
He said this means there is not much time before Europe faces a major change in security policy.

Finland could continue relying on the European Union, join NATO's planned enhanced Partnership for Peace programme, or opt for alliance with NATO to ensure Finland has a say in this new structure, he said.

"We have inherited a perception largely from the days of (former Swedish Prime Minister) Olof Palme that neutrality is somehow sacrosanct to Sweden -- that it could never be abandoned," he said. "That is a mistaken perception."
"For the Swedes belonging to the western community is self-evident," he said. "For us it has not been." REUTER
